Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: You, Cheap, City

outputs.L1:
“You look sleazy tonight,” Ma said.

“Cheap,” I said. “I’m doing cheap. Do you have any idea how much it costs to do cheap these days? To do gold City of Paris three-inch platform sandals and this I. Magnin snake dress? I’m doing cheap.”

“You look like a bird,” she said, “a Halloween bird with red waxed lips.”

In high school, you could either do cheap or Shakespeare, college prep or a pointy bra, ratting a bubble haircut with a toilet brush. I was not allowed to do high-school cheap; I did blazers and wool skirts from the Junior League thrift shop. In high school, it was: Don’t walk in the middle of Richie, Leelee, and the baby; you might come between them. You look like a skag wearing that black-eyed makeup; people are going to think you’re cheap.

While I poured red food dye on my hair to match my filly’s tail for the rodeo, Ma beat her head against the wall, she said, trying to make me nice.

“I tried real hard,” I said, “but the loggers, the Navy guys—they always hit on me.”

“Because you’re an easy mark,” Ma said.

And I played guilty. I played guilty every time.

“But now,” I said, “now I’m doing cheap.”
outputs.L2:
“You seem trashy tonight,” Ma said.

“Not trashy,” I told her. “Cheap. That’s the look I’m going for. Do you have any clue what it costs nowadays to look cheap? These gold three-inch platform sandals from City of Paris, this snakeskin dress from I. Magnin—I’m doing cheap.”

“You look like some kind of bird,” she said. “A Halloween bird, with those shiny red lips.”

In high school, the choices seemed to be cheap or Shakespeare, college prep or a pointed bra, teasing your bubble hairdo up with a toilet brush. I wasn’t permitted to be cheap in high school; I wore blazers and wool skirts bought at the Junior League thrift store. Back then it was, “Don’t walk between Richie, Leelee, and the baby—you might split them up.” Or, “You look like a skag with all that black eye makeup. People will think you’re cheap.”

When I poured red food coloring into my hair so it would match my filly’s tail for the rodeo, Ma banged her head against the wall and said she was only trying to make me decent. I did try, really hard, but the loggers and the Navy men kept coming on to me anyway.

“Because you’re an easy target,” Ma said.

And every time, I acted ashamed. I took the blame every time.

“But now,” I said, “now I’m choosing cheap.”

The narrator’s mother criticizes her appearance, describing it as sleazy and cheap. Her comments are not simply about clothing; they carry judgment, shame, and an attempt to define how the narrator should present herself to the world. To the mother, looking “cheap” suggests a lack of respectability, and she treats her daughter’s style as something embarrassing or improper.

The narrator, however, rejects this criticism. She insists that her appearance is intentional, not careless or accidental. In fact, she points out that “doing cheap” is expensive, suggesting that the look requires effort, taste, and money. What others dismiss as trashy or inappropriate is, for her, carefully constructed. She is not failing to meet a standard of femininity or respectability; she is choosing a different one.

This conflict has roots in the narrator’s high school years, when she remembers being pressured to dress in a more respectable way. She was encouraged to avoid looking cheap and to present herself in a manner that would be considered proper, controlled, and acceptable. These expectations taught her that appearance was closely tied to reputation, and that girls were often judged harshly for how they dressed.

Her mother played a major role in enforcing these expectations. She tried to control the narrator’s image, pushing her toward respectability and warning her against attracting the wrong kind of attention. At the same time, when men showed interest in the narrator, her mother blamed her for it, as if her clothing or appearance made her responsible for their behavior. This placed the burden on the narrator to manage not only how she looked, but also how others responded to her.

Now, the narrator embraces the cheap look as a deliberate form of self-expression. What was once used to shame or control her becomes something she claims for herself. By choosing to look sleazy or cheap on purpose, she challenges the idea that respectability should determine her worth. Her style becomes a way of asserting independence, rejecting her mother’s judgments, and taking ownership of her own image.
outputs.L4:
The narrator looks back on her adolescence through the charged language of clothing, makeup, and her mother’s disapproval. As a girl, she learns that appearance is never neutral. A skirt, a shade of lipstick, a pair of shoes, or the way she carries herself can all become evidence in her mother’s eyes: evidence of vulgarity, sexual availability, bad taste, or lower-class behavior. Her mother’s judgments are not simply about fashion. They are about femininity, sexuality, respectability, and class. To look “cheap” is to fail at being the kind of girl her mother wants her to be—controlled, modest, respectable, and safely distant from any sign of sexual independence.

The daughter remembers these judgments with anger as well as defiance. Her mother’s words have clearly wounded her, because they turned ordinary acts of self-expression into occasions for shame. Makeup and clothes, which might have been sources of pleasure or experimentation, became battlegrounds. The mother policed her daughter’s body and appearance as though femininity had to be carefully managed in order to protect social status. Behind the criticism lies fear: fear that the daughter will be seen as common, promiscuous, or improper; fear that she will cross the invisible boundaries that separate “respectable” womanhood from the women looked down upon as tasteless or sexually available.

Yet the narrator does not simply accept this lesson. As an adult, she deliberately embraces the very style her mother condemned. She chooses to “do cheap,” not because she is unaware of its meanings, but because she knows them too well. What was once used to shame her becomes something she can wear knowingly and proudly. By exaggerating or reclaiming the signs of cheapness—bold clothes, visible makeup, an unapologetic attitude—she refuses the idea that her worth depends on appearing tasteful, modest, or socially acceptable.

This act of self-presentation becomes a form of resistance. The narrator turns her body into a site of choice rather than obedience. She exposes the cruelty hidden inside standards of “good taste” and “proper” femininity, showing how those standards often discipline women by making them afraid of being judged. Her defiance is not merely aesthetic; it is emotional and political. She rejects the shame attached to classed and sexualized ideas of femininity, and in doing so, she reclaims power over the image of herself that her mother once tried to control.

The text therefore presents a fraught mother-daughter relationship shaped by judgment, shame, and rebellion. It shows how deeply social expectations can enter family life, especially through the policing of girls’ bodies and appearances. But it also shows that identity is not fixed by those judgments. By choosing the very look she was taught to despise, the narrator transforms “cheapness” from an insult into a declaration of independence. Her style becomes a language of refusal: a way of saying that she will not be made respectable at the cost of her own freedom.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a gritty first-person prose poem about a woman arguing with her mother over looking “cheap,” mixing fashion details, class resentment, teenage memories, and defiant humor.
counterfactuals.output:
My mother says I look cheap like she’s naming a disease, like I’ve come down with something you catch under bad fluorescent lights.

She says it from the kitchen table, where the plastic cloth is split at the corners and the salt shaker is shaped like a rooster. She says it while wearing her good blouse, the one with the pearl buttons, polyester pretending to be silk, Sunday pretending not to have a ladder in its tights. She pinches the air near my skirt like the hem has insulted her personally.

Too short, she says. Too tight. Too red. Too much eyeliner. Too much leg. Too much mouth.

I say, Ma, if I’m cheap, how come everything on me costs money?

The boots are secondhand but they have a heel like a threat. The fishnets have one run up the thigh and I let it stay there because some things are prettier when they admit what they’ve survived. My lipstick is drugstore crimson, named something stupid like Siren or Sin, and I bought it with coins from under the couch, nickels furred with lint and old shame. My jacket is fake leather, which is what we call things when they are honest about being poor.

She says, You want people to think you’re that kind of girl?

I laugh because mothers always believe there are kinds of girls, arranged like laundry: whites, colors, delicates, ruined.

What kind was I at fifteen, Ma, when you made me wear the beige dress to Aunt Lina’s wedding, the one that hung on me like a punishment? When my knees were bruised from climbing the fire escape and my bra strap kept slipping down and all the grown men looked away too late? What kind was I when I stole your mascara and drew myself new eyes in the bathroom mirror, black-rimmed and furious, while you banged on the door yelling we’d miss the bus?

We were always missing something. The bus. The rent. The sale at the supermarket. The chance to be people who didn’t have to worry how they looked carrying coupons.

She tells me, You don’t understand. The world sees a woman dressed like that and makes up its mind.

I tell her the world made up its mind when it saw our building, our hallway smelling like cabbage and damp coats, our last name mispronounced by teachers with clean fingernails. The world made up its mind when I got free lunch and hid the ticket in my sleeve. When I wore Payless shoes with cardboard soles in February and called them “new” because lying was warmer than socks. When girls with real gold hoops and mothers who drove cars asked if my sweater was vintage, and I said yes because vintage sounded better than dead lady from church basement.

Cheap, she says again, softer now, like she’s less angry at me than at the word.

And I know what she means. I do. She spent her life trying not to be mistaken for available, for desperate, for one missed paycheck from kneeling. She ironed collars until they shone. She kept her lipstick pale, her voice low, her legs crossed at the ankle like a locked gate. She taught me dignity the way other mothers teach recipes: add starch, remove desire, never let them smell hunger.

But I am all hunger, Ma.

I am hoop earrings big enough to jump through. I am glitter in the crease of a working-class eye. I am the clearance rack with a knife tucked in its garter. I am not expensive, but I am costly. There is a difference.

She says, Men will look.

I say, Let them. I’ve been looked at in school uniforms, winter coats, hospital gowns, pajamas at the bodega buying milk. A woman doesn’t need red lipstick to become a billboard for somebody else’s bad manners.

She sighs the sigh she brought with her from the old country, or the old neighborhood, or the old wound—wherever mothers keep their weather. She reaches for my skirt again, tugging it down an inch like that inch could save me from history.

I slap her hand, not hard. We both stare at the place where love just made a noise.

Then I grin, because if I don’t, I’ll cry, and my eyeliner is not waterproof; it’s aspirational.

Ma, I say, I don’t look cheap. I look like I know the price and refused to pay it.

She looks at me then. Really looks. At the boots, the red mouth, the run in the fishnets climbing toward my hip like a fuse. At her daughter, lit up all wrong and still burning.

For a second she almost smiles.

Then she says, At least take a sweater.

And because I am rebellious but not stupid, I take the damn sweater.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a raw, fragmented monologue in a 1970s punk/feminist literary style, where the narrator insists she is deliberately “doing cheap” despite her mother’s shame and criticism.
counterfactuals.output:
I’m doing cheap.

Say it like spit. Say it like a match struck on the sole of a boot.

Cheap lipstick, cheap rooms, cheap coffee burned black in a chipped cup. Cheap dress with the hem coming loose and I let it come loose. I help it. I pull the thread in the ladies’ room while some girl with blue eyelids watches me in the mirror like I’m a warning or a dare.

My mother says: shame.

My mother says: you were raised better.

My mother says: what will people think, walking around like that, talking like that, laughing with your mouth open, knees apart, hair hacked off like you lost a fight with yourself.

And I say: I did. I lost. Then I got up meaner.

I’m not fallen. I climbed down.

There’s a difference.

She wants good wool. Good manners. Good plates with flowers around the edge. She wants a daughter who knows how to lower her voice and cross the room without making history. A daughter who says thank you to men who pinch her future into shape. A daughter polished up for some fluorescent office, some clean kitchen, some bed where the sheets smell like surrender and detergent.

No.

I’m doing cheap.

On purpose.

Cheap is mine because nobody guards it. Nobody puts it in a velvet box and says don’t touch. Cheap is the streetlight buzzing. Cheap is the bus seat split open, yellow foam showing like guts. Cheap is a beer bought with coins and drunk too fast. Cheap is music from a basement with wet walls and girls screaming because nobody gave them permission and nobody can take it back.

My mother looks at me like I’ve sold something.

Maybe I have.

Maybe I sold the little white gloves. The Easter hat. The yes-ma’am. The “don’t make a scene.” The “he didn’t mean it.” The “boys will be boys.” The “nice girls don’t.”

Good riddance.

I traded it all for black nails, bad grammar, a room of my own even if it stinks of smoke and the radiator bangs all night like a drunk god. I traded it for my name in my own mouth. I traded it for hunger with teeth.

She says cheap like it’s a stain.

I say cheap like it’s a weapon.

I say: Mother, you taught me shame so well I can wear it inside out. Look. See the seams. See the labor. See the little hands sewing me shut.

I cut them.

I cut them with safety scissors, kitchen knives, song lyrics, other girls’ laughter, my own dirty jokes. I cut them badly. Jagged. Beautiful.

I am not your good fabric.

I am not your investment.

I am not the living proof that you suffered correctly.

I’m doing cheap because expensive things are always owned by somebody. Locked up. Insured. Displayed. Passed between men with clean hands and rotten mouths.

Cheap gets around.

Cheap survives.

Cheap can be lost and found and lost again. Cheap can bleed on the carpet and still go dancing. Cheap can say no. Cheap can say yes and mean it. Cheap can walk home alone at dawn with mascara down her face and not turn into a lesson.

My mother says I break her heart.

I say: was it yours, or was it built for you?

She cries into her good handkerchief. I smoke out the window. The neighbors hear us. Let them. Let the whole block hear. Let the priests and aunties and bosses and husbands hear. Let them press their ears to the wallpaper.

I am making a scene.

I am making myself.

Doing cheap, doing loud, doing wrong, doing alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short autobiographical-sounding scene: a mother says her daughter looks sleazy, and the daughter responds with a funny, bitter reflection on clothes, high school, makeup, rodeos, and being judged by men.
counterfactuals.output:
“You look sleazy,” my mother said, standing in the hallway with her coffee cup held like a gavel.

I looked down at myself: denim skirt, boots, too much eyeliner, a shirt I’d bought at the mall because it made me feel like someone who had somewhere to go. I was sixteen, which meant every outfit was either a cry for help or evidence for the prosecution.

“Sleazy?” I said. “Mom, this is just what girls wear when they’re trying not to look like they were raised in a feed store.”

She sighed like I’d personally invented shame.

The truth was, in high school, clothes were less about fashion than weatherproofing. You dressed for the climate of other people’s opinions. Too plain, and boys ignored you until they needed homework. Too pretty, and girls sharpened their voices. Too much makeup, and grown men at rodeos felt entitled to smile at you like they’d discovered something on sale.

I’d learned early that mascara was apparently a moral decision. Lipstick could rewrite your entire character. A skirt could turn you from honor-roll student into “that kind of girl” before first period.

At the rodeo, men in hats older than my childhood would look me up and down while pretending to admire the horses. At school, boys who couldn’t pass biology felt qualified to grade my body. And at home, my mother stood guard at the door, trying to save me from a world that had already made up its mind.

So I laughed, because otherwise I might have cried.

“Don’t worry,” I told her, grabbing my jacket. “If anyone judges me, I’ll just tell them I got it from my mama.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental passage with no quotation marks, colloquial dialogue, and stream-of-consciousness pacing about femininity, class, thrift-shop respectability, and choosing to look trashy on purpose.
counterfactuals.output:
I bought the red shoes because they looked like trouble somebody had donated after getting saved.

Patent peeling at the heel, little crescent moons of scuff on the toes, the kind of shoes that said I have cried in a bathroom stall and then gone back out anyway. Three dollars. Two ninety-nine if you want to be exact, and women like us are always exact with money, always counting the pennies like rosary beads, like proof we tried.

My mother would have said, You’re not leaving the house like that.

And I would have said, Watch me.

Except I never said Watch me. Not then. Back then I said, Fine. Back then I changed. Back then I learned the holy language of nice. Nice blouse. Nice slacks. Nice girl. Nice means nobody thinks you are hungry. Nice means the landlord calls you ma’am before raising the rent. Nice means the cashier doesn’t watch your hands. Nice means you have successfully disguised the emergency.

At the thrift store there is a whole aisle of emergencies ironed flat.

Church skirts. Interview skirts. Widow dresses. Secretary blouses with limp bows at the neck, beige and cream and that sad office pink. Clothes that say I am trying. Clothes that say please don’t confuse me with where I come from. Clothes that say I own a lint roller and a small fear of God.

I run my hand along them and feel all the women still inside.

Girl, that’s cute, says the woman beside me, holding up a fake fur jacket with a missing hook.

It’s ugly, I say.

That’s what I said. Cute.

We laugh because we know the difference is just rent.

Femininity, I think, standing there with my basket and my chipped nail polish, is mostly a costume department with bad lighting. Here is the good daughter cardigan. Here is the don’t touch me lipstick. Here is the I have a boyfriend flannel. Here is the I do not have a boyfriend and that is information you may die without knowing leather skirt. Here is the bra that makes you employable. Here is the bra that makes men stupid. Here is the bra that hurts, which is most of them, which is maybe the point.

A girl in the mirror keeps appearing and disappearing behind racks of denim. She has my face but meaner. Better eyebrows. She says, You could look respectable.

I say, I have.

She says, You could get the navy dress. The navy dress says benefits. The navy dress says dental. The navy dress says no drama.

I say, I am full of drama. It has to go somewhere.

The loudest dress in the store hangs by the fitting rooms like it has been waiting to insult me personally. Animal print but not any animal God made. Leopard after a gas leak. Tiger if the tiger worked at a bowling alley. Stretchy, too short, synthetic, clinging to the hanger with a cheap electric sadness. The neckline plunges like a bad decision. The hem curls up already, eager to embarrass.

I want it immediately.

Not because it is pretty. Pretty is a prison with curtains. Pretty behaves. Pretty asks permission from the room and then thanks the room for having eyes. I don’t want pretty. I want visible from a moving car. I want every auntie in a five-mile radius to inhale sharply. I want men to think whatever dumb thing they think and then realize I am not asking. I want the old spell reversed. If they’re going to call us trash for being poor, for being loud, for being soft in the wrong places, for buying generic cereal, for having mothers with tired hands and fathers who disappeared into work or drink or both, then fine. Fine. I will arrive glittering at the dump like the queen of it.

The fitting room curtain doesn’t close all the way. It never does. There’s always that little mercy gap where the world can peek in and judge your back fat, your underwear, the tattoo you got when you were nineteen and believed in escape as a place instead of a behavior.

You good in there? the clerk calls.

Yeah, I say, fighting the dress over my hips. Just negotiating.

It snaps into place.

I look like a problem.

I look like the girl mothers warn their sons about, which is funny because those sons are usually the danger. I look cheap, but cheap like a blade bought at a gas station. Cheap like strong perfume in August. Cheap like payday cash folded into a bra. Cheap like surviving has stripped the varnish off and left the wood exposed.

And underneath that, or inside that, or maybe because of that, I look expensive to myself.

Not wealthy. Never that. Wealthy is quiet. Wealthy is beige linen and not knowing the bus schedule. Wealthy is calling clutter eclectic. Wealthy is wearing ripped jeans that cost more than my electric bill and being praised for authenticity. I am not wealthy. I am clearance rack incarnate. I am the last size. I am missing button, final sale, all proceeds benefit someone else’s idea of charity.

But I can choose.

That is the small violent luxury.

I can choose the red shoes. I can choose the trash dress. I can choose earrings big enough to pick up radio signals from dead divas. I can choose hair sprayed high, mouth painted dark, hoops like door knockers, nails like candy, a purse with rhinestones shedding in my lap. I can choose to look like what they already think and make it theatrical, make it mine, make it too much for their little clipboard categories.

Because respectability is so expensive.

It costs tailoring. It costs posture. It costs never saying ain’t even when ain’t is the truest word in the sentence. It costs smiling at women who clutch their bags near you. It costs lowering your voice. It costs smoothing your hair. It costs pretending your mother’s accent is not music. It costs pretending you did not learn math from coupons, grief from the kitchen table, glamour from the women outside the club at 1 a.m. smoking in heels with their whole lives showing.

Baby, my aunt would say, there’s looking poor and there’s acting poor. Don’t do both.

But what if I do both beautifully.

What if I act poor with rhythm. What if I laugh too loud because joy has bad manners. What if I wear gold that turns my skin green and call the green a garden. What if I stop auditioning for people who would only love me as a lesson. What if femininity isn’t a clean white slip but a leopard thing with a broken zipper, sweat under the arms, red mouth on a cigarette butt, perfume and fryer grease and hope all mixed up. What if I am not failing womanhood. What if womanhood is failing to keep up with me.

The clerk rings me up. Dress, shoes, fake pearls, one black slip I tell myself is practical. Twelve forty-six.

You got somewhere to wear all this? she asks.

I say, The grocery store if I feel like it.

She grins. As you should.

Outside, the afternoon is gray and judgmental. Cars hiss by. Somebody’s baby is screaming from a stroller, pure opera, no shame yet. I sit at the bus stop with my plastic bag between my knees, and I can feel the dress inside it like a dare with a heartbeat.

An old man looks at my red shoes, then at me.

Those are something, he says.

I say, So am I.

The bus comes sighing and kneeling to the curb, tired as the rest of us. I climb on, three dollars poorer and somehow richer, holding my bag of donated trouble, my secondhand armor, my trashy little crown.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a confessional literary vignette in the voice of a rebellious daughter recalling her mother calling her cheap, her attempts to be “nice,” and her eventual embrace of the label.
counterfactuals.output:
My mother first called me cheap in the kitchen, where all our family prophecies were delivered over the sink.

I remember the yellow light, the fat blue dish soap, her wrists moving in circles inside the steam. She did not look at me when she said it. That was the worst part. If she had looked, I could have met her eyes and made a performance of injury. I could have slammed a door, rehearsed my tragedy, turned the insult into proof of her cruelty and my purity. But she said it as if she were naming a stain.

Cheap.

Because my skirt was too short, or my laugh too loud, or because a boy with a car had idled outside and I had gone running before he honked twice. Because I wore lipstick the color of a bitten plum. Because I wanted things. Not even expensive things—just things with glitter, things with straps, things that promised an evening could be peeled open like fruit.

For years I tried to be nice.

Nice was a pale cardigan. Nice was knees together on the bus. Nice was saying thank you when men interrupted me, sorry when women disliked me, yes when no had already lit a match in my throat. I practiced softness like piano scales. I lowered my voice. I bought blouses with collars. I learned to smile without showing hunger.

My mother praised these efforts in small, rationed ways. “That’s better,” she would say, as if I were a hem she had taken up. “You look decent.” Decent was her idea of love: nothing showing, nothing owed.

But niceness sat on me badly. It pinched. It made me mean in secret. I envied girls who tossed their hair and spent their money and kissed as if kissing were not a legal confession. I envied their shamelessness, not knowing yet that shame was something women were trained to mistake for a spine.

Then one night—there is always one night in stories like this, though really it was many nights, accumulating—I caught my reflection in a shop window. Red mouth, cheap earrings, eyes bright with having disobeyed. I looked exactly like the girl my mother had warned me against.

And I loved her.

Not tenderly. Not with forgiveness. I loved her with the fierce relief of recognition.

Cheap, then. Let it be cheap. Let me be rhinestone, drugstore perfume, black tights laddered at the knee. Let me be the bargain-bin daughter, marked down and touched by many hands, still gleaming under fluorescent light. Let nice girls keep their receipts and their clean names. I had paid enough in silence.

When my mother said the word again years later, softer this time, almost weary—cheap—I did not flinch.

I heard what she meant: unguarded, unowned, too willing to glitter.

I smiled at her across the table.

“Yes,” I said. “And look how much I shine.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
